headline: "Oh, shut up." Three days later, Jackson says: no regrets.
summary: Troy Jackson told Susan Collins to "shut up" in Thursday's Maine Senate debate, after she called a heckler "obviously one of Troy's supporters." On CNN Sunday he said he won't apologize: "I'm not going to be talked down to." Collins called the reply "very telling" and raised his temper in the Legislature. Maine votes November 3.

cover_question.q: Does he have to say sorry?

cover_answer: No rule makes him. He won't. Voters grade it November 3.
table_question: If you were right, do you still have to say sorry for being rude?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Two grown-ups in Maine want the same job, and on TV last week, while a man in the crowd kept shouting, one of them told the other "Oh, shut up." On Sunday he said he isn't sorry. At our table you would say sorry, like picking up a block tower you knocked over. The grown-ups in Maine pick between them in two weeks.
5-7.why: One rude line, one rule they already know, and who decides. At six, "shut up" is a rule they police at home, so the script starts there.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the one line they already know is against the rules, a block tower to put back, and who picks in the end. The temper stories can wait. Expect "does he get a time-out?" No. Grown-ups get a vote instead.

8-12.script: Thursday a protester yelled while Susan Collins spoke. She said he was "obviously" Troy Jackson's supporter. Jackson said "Oh, shut up," and Sunday he said he won't apologize. A debate has a moderator, not a referee: no penalty, so Maine's voters score it on November 3.
8-12.why: Heckler, accusation, snap, no penalty. The voters are the referee. This age wants to know who enforces the rule.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules, fairness and whether adults keep them, so the script runs the chain: a heckler, an accusation without proof, a snap, and no referee to call it. That gap is the mechanism, and the vote fills it. Expect "who was right?" Say that both broke a rule at the table and let them rank the two.

13-17.script: Who started it? Collins pinned a heckler on Jackson with no proof; he told her to "shut up" and says he'd do it again. Second: Collins calls the reply "very telling" about how he treats women he disagrees with. Does a pattern change how one line reads?
13-17.why: Who started it, then whether a pattern changes one line. Teenagers can weigh provocation against response, so give them both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: Collins took a cheap shot, and Jackson's reply was rude. The script asks who started it, then whether his record in the Legislature changes how one line reads. Kuhn calls argument a practised skill, so let them split the blame. Expect "would you have said it?" Answer honestly.

5-7.q: Is he in trouble for saying shut up?
5-7.a: No time-out for grown-ups. People saw it, and they will decide what they think of it when they vote.

8-12.q: Does he have to say sorry?
8-12.a: No rule makes him. He says he won't. Maine votes November 3.

8-12.q: Was the shouting man really his supporter?
8-12.a: He says he had no idea who it was. A climate group says it was theirs.

13-17.a: She had no proof. A cheap shot and a hot reply can both be true.

13-17.q: Does refusing to apologize win votes?
13-17.a: Nobody knows yet. Collins is already using the line against him.
